title: What If 86% of a Country's Cash Was Cancelled Overnight? India Did It

scenes.text: What if most of the cash in your wallet stopped being money tonight? In 2016, India's did.
At 8 p.m. on November 8th, the prime minister went on television. The 500 and 1,000 rupee notes were void, effective immediately.
That was 86 percent of all the cash in a country where about nine in ten purchases were made in cash.
For weeks, people queued at banks and cash machines to swap old notes for new ones.
The aim was to wipe out hidden, untaxed money that its owners wouldn't dare bring to a bank.
Two years later the central bank finished counting. 99.3 percent of the cancelled notes had come back.

description:
What if most of a country's cash stopped being money overnight? At 8 pm on 8 November 2016, India's prime minister announced that 500 and 1,000 rupee notes were withdrawn with immediate effect.
Those notes made up 86 percent of the currency in circulation by value, in an economy where around 90 percent of everyday transactions were in cash. The stated aims were to hit undeclared black money and counterfeit notes. People queued at banks and ATMs for weeks, and the cost of printing new notes more than doubled. In its annual report of August 2018 the Reserve Bank of India said 99.3 percent of the cancelled notes, 15.31 lakh crore rupees, had been returned to banks.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Printing the replacement notes cost the central bank more than twice its usual yearly bill. How long would you last without cash? Drop your own what-if below.
